newsitem.title: INDIA: India RBI promotes bank rate to market signal role.
newsitem.headline: India RBI promotes bank rate to market signal role.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Tuesday said it will use its bank rate to signal future changes in its monetary stance.
"As far as we are concerned, it is an indicative rate to send signals," RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan said on Tuesday.
Previously the bank rate was regarded as relatively unimportant, but in future it will act as a guide to moves in commercial banks' prime lending rates.
"We do think as the bank rates change, so will the PLR chage," Rangarajan told a news conference. "We are reformulating everything in terms of the bank rate."
RBI cut its bank rate, defined as the lowest rate at which the bank lends money, to 11 percent from 12 percent.

RBI said it would now peg the following to the bank rate; advances to state governments, state corporations, overdrafts, penal rates on shortfalls in reserve requirements, concessional export credit finance and advances to cooperative banks and primary dealers.
"It will start softening earlier than expected," the governor said, in response to a question when he expected banks to cut lending rates.
Both State Bank of India and Corporation Bank cut their PLRs from 14.5 percent to 14.0 percent following the RBI announcement.
The RBI also announced a reduction in the cap on interest on deposits up to one year by two percentage points below the bank rate to 9.0 percent per annum, down from the earlier 10.0 percent.

The deposit cut was part of the steps announced by the RBI in its 1997/98 (April-March) monetary policy announced earlier on Tuesday. Immediately after the announcement, the state-run Corporation Bank said it was cutting its prime lending rate to 14.0 percent per annum from 14.5 percent.
Rangarajan said the removal of reserve requirements on inter-bank borrowing and steps to deepen the forex market would help integrate the money market with the external market.
He said this would give birth to a rupee yield curve.
Abolition of banks' cash reserve requirement on inter-bank borrowings was a long-standing demand of many Indian banks which said this was standing in the way of creation of a term money market.
Rangarajan said long-term interest rates would fall only when the economy sees inflation sustained at a lower level.
Broad money (M3) growth of 15.0-15.5 percent coupled with a real growth of the economy at 6.0-7.0 percent would help contain inflation at around 6.0 percent, he said.
RBI said it aimed at greater integration of the money market with the foreign exchange market.

For the first time, RBI said it would allow authorised foreign exchange dealers to borrow upto $10.0 million from their foreign offices or correspondents without any condition on end-use and repayment of these borrowings.
Foreign exchange dealers would also be allowed to invest in overseas money market instruments for the first time, RBI said.
Analysts said the RBI's moves meshed with India's programme of economic reforms.
